content.thinking:
I'm planning out the gnome model: a low-poly whimsical figure about 1.1m tall with faceted, flat-colored parts, and sketching the skeleton hierarchy starting from the hips root joint through the spine chain.

Mapping overall proportions: short stocky legs, a chubby torso, an oversized head, and a tall floppy hat tip, aiming for a total height around 1.2 meters while keeping the design clearly gnome-like. Working through joint placements using absolute coordinates to avoid orientation issues, defining the spine as a curved chain rather than straight segments.

For the neck and head, I'm deciding between a short chain with named tip joints versus explicit individual joints for neck, head, and jaw, leaning toward direct joints parented off the last spine joint for clearer control over orientation.

For the torso surface, I'm working out how to loft across the spine bone path, debating whether to include the hips joint in the bone list since it shares the same position as the first spine joint, and deciding to just use the spine chain alone to avoid ambiguous overlapping stations.

I'll go with a simpler shift constant to keep the belly shape manageable, and favor moderate complexity over risky intricate API calls since type correctness matters most. For the body sections I'm considering a low-poly faceted look using flattened circle facets rather than smooth curves, defining a small tube helper to keep things consistent.

For colors, I'm sketching a whimsical palette -- warm skin tone with a rosy nose, off-white beard, and a red hat -- and thinking through how to add candy-cane style stripes to the hat using a swept path with banded coloring based on position along the sweep.

Thinking further on the story: the hat could have a thin yellow brim band with cream star decals, plus a brown leather buckle strap and brass-ringed goggles pushed up on top for a tinkerer vibe. For the outfit, I'm weighing a classic gnome look against a tinkerer theme -- settling on a red hat, teal-green tunic, and a tan leather apron.

Now I'm picking the rest of the palette: purple trousers for a whimsical touch, brown boots, brass and steel accents, a glowing blue glass element, plus green buttons, pink cheeks, and dark eyes, keeping the total flat colors under 64. I'm starting to lay out the skeleton, defining hip and leg joint positions for the pose.

So with 3 points we get 2 spans: hipL to kneeL, kneeL to ankleL, with the tip being the ankle joint. Then for the foot, I'll add a toe joint parented to the ankle bone, probably giving it a "digit" role. For mirroring, I'll loop over side signs where +1 is left (x=0.09) and -1 is right, keeping conventions consistent with the local coordinate frame.

Now I'm computing arm placement for an A-pose: shoulder, elbow, and wrist positions, working out direction vectors and lengths for the upper arm and forearm so the arms angle down and slightly forward rather than sticking straight out horizontally.

Designing the hands as rounded mitt palms with simple finger chains—three fingers plus a thumb per hand, each a two-joint segment parented to the wrist bone, keeping joint counts manageable.

Working out finger orientation now, computing a forward direction from elbow to wrist and fanning the fingers in a plane that curls them slightly forward.

Still working out finger geometry...

Keeping hands skin-toned with brown leather wrist cuffs and brass details. I'm shaping the palm as a flattened low-poly icosahedron attached at the wrist joint. Since rest pose needs neutral extended hands, tools like the hammer, wrench, and screwdriver stay stowed in belt loops instead of being held, and now I'm positioning the head joint.

I'm placing the neck and head joints with upward-pointing bone orientations, then sizing an oversized cartoon head slightly flattened front-to-back to sit atop the torso. I'm working out overall proportions—legs, torso, and head segments—and positioning the floppy hat base and tip so the whole figure reads as a gnome around 1.25-1.3 meters tall.

I'm now plotting a curved chain of points for the hat that droops backward and down, tapering radius smoothly from base to tip across four joint segments parented to the head.

Rather than a floppy brim, I'll give the gnome hat a turned-up cuff ring, maybe adding a small bell or pom at the tip using a lathe outline with radius widening slightly from 0.14 to 0.19.

For the brim I'll lathe a closed loop of points forming a small ring shape with 10 flat-shaded segments. For the hat's color, I'm thinking a custom paint function for red with darker mottling and a thin spiraling yellow stripe.

Now I'm adding a brass gear decal to the front of the hat, applied along the sweep surface.

Then I'm positioning goggles on the hat too—two brass torus rings with blue lens discs and a strap—working out their placement near the hat's base cone so the lenses sit against the front surface.

Still placing the strap loop...

Now for the face: big whimsical eyes with white spheres, dark pupils, and highlights; bushy white eyebrow sweeps; a bulbous pink-red nose; and a white beard built as a loft along a chin-descending chain with varying width.

I need to check that the beard stations don't collide with the chest geometry at those z-depths.

With torso depth settled, I'll texture the beard with white-to-cream grain streaks running along the length, and consider adding a few triangular spike-like locks for a tufted, low-poly feel. For the mustache, I'll sweep two curved white tubes outward from the nose sides.

Moving to the ears, I'm placing pointy spike cones angled outward and slightly forward for a gnome look, with small pink inner-ear spikes. I'm also adding flattened pink blush spheres on the cheeks, and working out how to build a simple lower jaw/chin piece since the mouth itself will be mostly hidden by the mustache and beard.

I'm deciding to model the head as an upper skull sphere with cheeks, plus a separate squashed lower jaw piece riding a jaw joint pivot so the beard can be parented to it and open naturally. I'm placing a small dark flattened ellipse under the mustache to suggest the mouth opening, tucked against the jaw.

I'll shrink the mouth and raise the mustache so a smile gap peeks through, defining a dark curved sweep for the mouth line riding the jaw bone, then setting up the jaw joint and lower jaw part so it parents correctly. Now I'm thinking about adding tunic clothing as a sweep over the spine chain, slightly larger than the body radius.

Still writing clothing details...

I'm computing the ellipse radii and front-surface offsets at each torso height, tracking how the belly curve shifts the apron's z-position outward as it moves up from waist to shoulder.

Switching approach: instead of extruding a flat plane for the apron (which would clip into the bulging belly), I'm considering sweeping a thin box cross-section along a vertical path draped onto the front surface, letting the drape handle the normal offset while the box's width and thickness stay constant.

To fix the belly poking through, I'll push the apron plane further out to z=0.232 with 0.014 thickness so it clears the belly's max point, leaving a believable hanging gap near the top that reads like a strap-held apron. Now I'm shaping the outline itself: a narrower bib near the neck widening down to a scalloped hem, tracing the x-y coordinates to keep it cross-checked against the belt line.

For the texture, I'll apply a tan leather grain paint along the y-axis and add small pocket boxes stitched onto the apron's surface for detail.

I'm planning pocket placement and dimensions, then filling them with protruding tool shapes like screwdriver handles, pliers, a ruler, and pencils for realism. I also need to check that the apron hem sits correctly relative to the hips and thighs so the leg geometry lines up, and I'm considering skipping a flared tunic hem in favor of a simpler lathe shape.

Now I'm working out the skirt geometry as a lathe frustum around the hips, defining the outline points for the radius taper and belt placement to keep it from clashing with the apron's flat plane.

I'm checking whether the belt clips through the apron's surface — pushing the belt outward with extra lift so it sits in front rather than intersecting, adjusting its z-position relative to the apron's front edge.

I'll settle on the belt as a simple tube with a hexagonal cross-section, radius 0.02, covering the apron since it sits in front. Then I'm adding a brass buckle box positioned just beyond the belt's front face, with a dark inset for the hole, and starting to place tool loops like a hammer hanging at the hip.

Now I'm positioning the hammer's head and handle against the torso, adding a wrench on the other side, a leather pouch with a flap and brass stud at the left hip, and planning the backpack as a larger leather/wood frame attached to the chest joint at the back.

The pack's height works fine against the shoulders, fitting the gnome tinkerer theme with an oversized pack loaded with gear. Now I'm thinking about painting the backpack with leather grain and patchwork textures, plus adding a hinged lid flap at the top rear as a separate joint.

Adding lid and strap geometry...

The torso surface handles the drape fine since the path start snaps onto the nearest torso point regardless, with the pack covering that area, and the strap stays clear of the arms since it runs inboard of the shoulder. Now I'm turning to the backpack's attached gadgets and details.

For the telescoping antenna, I'm setting up a hinge joint with a rod running up from the pack top toward a small lathe-built dish, angled so it clears the hat tip which droops to the side. For the spinning rotor on top, I'm placing a hinge joint for a vertical shaft topped with a three-blade copter rotor.

Writing rotor blade geometry...

I'm checking the rotor's position so it doesn't collide with the hat — the blade radius and axis placement need to clear the hat's tip and chain, which means verifying the z and y ranges don't overlap near the head.

Checking the gap again at a shifted x position, it's tight but workable if I shrink the blade radius slightly and nudge the axis back. Shoulder and arm positions look clear of the pack. Now I'm thinking about placing a small cylindrical tank near the pack's side, checking it won't collide with the arm's swing range.

Let me plan the right side of the pack: mounting a copper tank vertically with brass bands and a gauge dial decal on the back, connected to the pack via curved pipe sweeps with valves. On the opposite side I'm considering tool bundles or a rolled blueprint scroll tied with ribbon, positioning it along the bottom of the pack instead of the top so it doesn't conflict with the lid.

Now I'm working out the gauge placement—a small dial decal with a brass bezel ring on the back, and thinking through a hanging lantern attached to the pack's side via a swinging hinge joint, with a cage frame and glow element inside.

I'm also considering extra flourishes: a tiny clockface, a sideways horn like a gramophone bell on the top-left, and a coiled brass spring using a spiral sweep path standing upright on the pack's right side.

I'll also add a brass gear on the back, extruded from a gear-tooth polygon outline and mounted low at the pack's rear.

Writing gear outline function...

I'm skipping shoulder pads for simplicity and moving to the boots, designing chunky rounded gnome boots with curled-up toes using a swept capsule shape from heel to toe with varying radii, plus a curved toe path for the characteristic curl.

Now I'm adding the sole as a thin frustum box sitting flush with the ground for proper foot contact, and planning a cuff ring at the ankle using a tapered cylinder to finish off the boot top.

For the leg itself, I'll sweep the trouser profile down with a slight taper from thigh to ankle, then work out how to place a knee patch decal—trying to figure out the right clock-angle convention on the leg sweep so the patch lands on the front of the knee where it bends forward.

For the torso, I'm settling on a teal mottled paint for the tunic rather than stripes, and thinking about whether brass buttons on the chest would even be visible above the apron bib.

I realize the beard already covers most of the upper chest, which would hide a neck collar or neckerchief anyway, so a simple cream collar ring is fine even if obscured. But I need to check the beard doesn't visually clash with the apron bib — the beard front extends to z .27, which pokes past the apron's z .239, so I'll need to adjust depths to avoid the collision.

Shifting the beard's z-center to .26 for the upper portion so it floats cleanly above the apron. Now I'm mapping out beard stations along the chin and jawline — defining width, height, and depth coordinates at several y-levels to taper the shape naturally into the chin, checking it aligns with the head sphere's front curvature at the jaw.

I'm setting the beard as its own joint chain parented to the jaw, with five stations forming five spans, and considering whether to assign it a skeletal role or leave it roleless as a simple decorative chain. I'm also sketching in small decorative touches — spike tufts, a braided tie band, maybe a brass bead or ribbon ring around the beard.

For the tuft texture, I'm thinking about scattering tiny cones across the beard surface, but worrying that cones pointing outward along the surface normal would look like thorns rather than hair spikes, so I may need a different approach to get a believable fuzzy texture.

Instead I'll try a grain paint pattern for subtle beard waves, and add three small spike extrusions at the beard's bottom tip pointing downward to create a zigzag, braided-looking end. Next I need to work out fluffy white eyebrows using a swept curve shape.

Now I'm checking placement math so the hat brim, head sphere, and eyes all line up correctly without the brim covering the eyes or the hat floating off the head's surface.

I'm computing eye and pupil sphere positions so they sit protruding just enough from the head surface, then sizing the nose to bulge out proportionally, and starting to lay out the mustache curve beneath the nose with symmetric side sweeps.

Now I'm placing the jaw and mouth: a scaled icosphere for the lower jaw, a dark flattened ellipse tucked under the mustache for the mouth interior, skipping a separate smile line since the dark mouth shape covers it.

Moving to the ear, I'm building it from spike primitives: an outer spike anchored near the head's side with a given direction and length, plus a smaller pink inner spike offset slightly forward to suggest the ear's inner cavity, computing endpoint positions from the direction vector and length.

Checking the geometry, the inner pink cone sits slightly in front of the outer ear cone's surface, so it remains visible rather than being hidden inside it. The hat brim covers the top of the head while the ears poke out sideways below its edge, so no overlap issues there. Now I'm shifting to the arms, setting up tapering sleeve radii that narrow from shoulder to wrist along the arm's chain of segments.

Adding a leather cuff ring near the wrist, oriented along the forearm direction and sized to wrap snugly. Since the arm's joint chain has shoulder, elbow, and wrist points, I'm deciding to bind the cuff explicitly to the elbow joint's bone and the hand parts to the wrist joint, rather than letting it auto-select the nearest bone, to avoid ambiguity at the overlap zone near the wrist.

Now I'm thinking through rolled sleeves with a cream cuff ending at the elbow, bare tan forearm skin below it, and a single continuous sweep along the arm chain with varying radius and a color band switch from sleeve teal to skin tone partway down, so the mesh bends smoothly through the elbow without a seam.

Placing that elbow cuff requires positioning and orienting it using the chain's point and tangent at t=0.5 — passing the chain frame directly into the part so the cylinder axis aligns with the arm direction and the skin weighting blends naturally through the bend.

For the arm path with shoulder, elbow, and wrist as a three-point polyline, I'm assuming the sweep smooths the corner so the skin stays continuous rather than faceted, with t=0.5 landing roughly at the elbow given the segment lengths. I can apply the same chain-based approach for the legs, sweeping trouser geometry over the leg chain with color bands transitioning toward the knee.

Legs taper from a wider upper-thigh radius down toward the ankle, with trousers in purple getting a vertical pinstripe pattern using a lighter purple accent, oriented so the stripe axis runs along x to create vertical lines rather than horizontal bands. Now I'm moving on to the pelvis, planning a sphere shape to connect the hip area into the torso.

I'm checking where the shoulder sockets should sit relative to the torso's radius so the arm sweeps overlap cleanly rather than leaving a gap, adjusting the shoulder x-position outward slightly to ensure the arm cap touches the torso surface, then recalculating the elbow position along that same sweep direction.

Writing torso radius function...

Now I'm sketching the neck as a short cylinder sweep with a bone-like taper, then positioning the head joint above it so the head parts sit relative to that anchor point.

For the head I'm skipping gloves and keeping fingers simple, using a subtle mottled skin paint with pink tones for blush and a red nose. The head shape itself I'm building from a low-detail icosahedron, scaled slightly to flatten it and painted with flat shading using its existing UVs.

Hands stay flat-colored with no paint, and now I'm working out the hammer: a rod-shaped wooden handle with a steel box head, positioned hanging from the belt on the character's side, tilted so the head sits up near the belt and the handle extends downward.

Adding a leather pouch with a brass stud on the left side, a wrench hanging at the back formed from simple boxes, and apron pockets holding a yellow screwdriver and red-handled pliers poking up above the pocket line.

Actually two separate pockets with a stitch divider works better. Now thinking about placing a screwdriver tool inside the pocket, but its cylinder handle at the given position would collide with the belt's z-range, so I need to either lower the pocket or reposition the tool so it doesn't poke through the belt geometry.

Trying lower pocket placement near the apron hem so tools stick up just enough to peek above, but they'd be mostly hidden behind the belt. Considering a chest pocket on the bib instead, but that area conflicts with where the beard hangs down, so I'd need to shorten the beard — though the long beard is pretty core to the gnome look, so I'll keep pockets low and just let small tool-handle stubs peek out above the belt line.

Instead I'll add side pockets as belt loops holding a hammer and wrench, with the lower apron pockets getting decorative stitched decals (screwdriver silhouettes) and brass rivet details at the corners using small merged spheres. I'll also add a measuring tape and mallet on the belt and goggles on the hat, then design SVG textures — starting with a round gauge/dial face with cream color, tick marks, a red warning zone, and a needle pointing toward it.

Writing the dial texture code...

For applying it, I'm using a circular geometry part so the UV mapping covers the full dial drawing cleanly. For the hat, I'm adding a gear-shaped decal patch positioned near the front brim, angled to match the hat's backward lean, with a defined position and size. I'm also placing goggles on a hat band near the base, slightly raised at the front.

Still working out goggle and strap placement...

Checking the brim coverage over the hat base and head position, then verifying goggle lens placement sits correctly against the strap front, since the z-depth math suggests they might clip slightly.

I'm shaping a small brass bell to dangle from the drooping hat tip, lathing its profile and adding a tiny clapper sphere, positioned at the hat's end point along its tangent direction.

I'm defining the hat's curved joint chain with four points sweeping upward then drooping downward at the tip, refining the exact coordinates for a natural floppy bend.

For the hat's paint I'm defining a diagonal stripe function based on dorsal clock position, alternating cream and base hat color for a spiral candy-cane effect. I'm also thinking through texel density across all the painted regions—hat, torso, legs, head, beard, backpack, apron—targeting roughly 2mm resolution given the total surface area.

Deciding to keep the paint atlas at the default 1024 resolution rather than bumping to 2048, since the stitched details don't need that much fidelity. For the backpack I'm sketching a leather-grain paint function that defines rectangular patches in absolute meter coordinates, with a dashed stitch border rendered near each patch edge.

Writing patch and stitch logic...

I'm placing the back-facing patches, deciding which faces get painted when viewed from behind, and planning the lid geometry with its hinge joint positioned at the rear of the box.

Now I'm working out the rotor mast mounted on the lid, with its hub joint and three blades positioned above, plus figuring out where to attach side gear like the copper tank onto the pack's left and right sides.

For the left tank I'm placing a vertical copper cylinder with a domed cap, brass bands, bolts, and a valve, then routing a steam pipe from the tank's cap up and over toward the pack top.

I'm checking whether the antenna rod placement clears the rotor sweep radius, repositioning it to the left front so it doesn't collide with the rotor blades while keeping it distinct from the pipe route.

Setting up the antenna as a two-joint hinge chain with tapering rod radii, then starting a lathe profile for a small dish bowl at the top.

Dish orientation aims outward with a forward-up facing direction, colored copper, with a small feed horn detail. The hat's rotor and antenna placement stay clear of each other, so now I'm shifting to the right side pack to place a spring coil component.

Working on the telescope placement — angling it diagonally along the pack's right side so it clears the shoulder joint, pointing forward with brass segments and a leather grip.

Now I'm adding a rolled blueprint scroll tied with ribbon, placed horizontally under the pack, then checking it against the skirt back for overlap and nudging its position to avoid clipping.

For the lantern, I'm trying to work out a good placement point since the obvious spots conflict with the telescope and oxygen tank already on the pack — considering a hook or curved pole extending from the pack's upper rear to hold it clear of those other items.

I'm trying a curved lamp pole arching forward from the pack over the shoulder, with the lantern glowing beside the head for a cute silhouette effect, but then I run into the antenna and rotor positions clashing — so I'm repositioning the rotor more centrally and shifting the antenna to the opposite side to keep clearance between the blades, hat, and head.

Checking the lantern position against the hat brim, ear tip, and shoulder to make sure nothing overlaps, then setting up the swing joint at the pole tip with a hinge pointing downward for the ring, chain, and cage parts of the lantern body.

I'm placing the glowing glass box, pyramid cap, and corner posts for the lantern cage, then routing a copper pipe from the tank cap to the mast while checking clearances against the pole rod, and adding a small valve wheel torus on the pipe before moving to the chest harness straps.

I'm adding cross-chest buckle straps, a side tool pouch with a pipe wrench and a few tool handles poking out, plus rivet details sampled around the pack's front rim using merged spheres.

I still need a gear-patch texture for the hat, plus finer facial touches like eyelids, brows, a nose highlight, and freckles.

Now I'm setting up the lantern's flame and lens glow import, and making sure joint names and roles follow rigging conventions—neck, head, jaw, spine chain rooted at hips with explicit parenting. Starting to write the joint and chain definitions...

Defining sweep options and build function...

Building the spine chain with three named joints, then sweeping the torso mesh over it using an octagonal cross-section with flat shading. I'm checking how the rounded cap at the bottom extends past the path end by the radius, which affects where the torso's bottom edge actually sits.

Actually the cap overshoot pushes the torso bottom too low into the leg zone, creating an oversized rump. I should switch to a flat start cap and adjust where the spine path begins so the skirt geometry properly covers the transition.

For the top end, a rounded cap would push the dome height into the head region, so I need to check whether it stays hidden behind the beard and hat or whether a flat end cap at the shoulder line is safer, even though that leaves the shoulder open.

Tuning the torso radius curve for a whimsical belly shape, then working out the apron depth and belt placement so the front sits proportionally with the lift from the belt loop.

Checking the belt and skirt radii against the torso curve at different heights, they line up closely enough that the belt covers the skirt's top edge with margin to spare. The apron sits further out than the torso and skirt at mid-body height, floating just slightly away, which should work fine for layering with the beard and front details.

Now I'm working through the arm sweep radii, tapering from shoulder to wrist with a color band switch from teal sleeve to skin tone at the midpoint, plus a cream cuff cylinder sized to hide that seam. I'm deciding to keep the sweep at 6 sides with sharp edges rather than smoothing, for a crisper low-poly look.

For the sleeve surface, I want a mottled teal texture matching the torso rather than stripes, since stripes along the arm's axis would wrap wrong around the limb geometry.

For the legs, I'm setting the hip and knee target positions so the limb bends forward slightly, then checking the reach distance stays within the segment lengths — maybe lengthening the segments a bit for a more pronounced bend.

I'm building the leg chain by converting the limb points into a polyline attached to the hips, naming each joint (hip, knee, ankle) and tagging it as a leg role, with the side determined by which direction x offsets. For the sweep radii tapering down the leg toward the ankle, I'm leaving room for the boot to cover the bottom, and keeping the default rounded caps since the top will be hidden inside the skirt anyway.

Now I'm defining the boot: a tapered foot sweep from heel to toe with varying radii, then a cylindrical shaft wrapping the ankle joint, plus a folded cuff at the top in a lighter leather tone, matching the gnome's brown boots with small brass buckle boxes on the sides. I'm also checking the sole geometry to make sure the boot bottom and the floor-contact sole box stay within the allowed tolerance so the foot doesn't visibly float or clip through the ground.

Setting up the arm chain generically for left and right sides now, defining shoulder, elbow, and wrist positions and building a skeletal chain parented to the spine joint.

Setting palm radius bigger at .055, then sketching out finger definitions with spread direction and per-finger offsets...

Simplifying to a cartoon hand with 3 fingers plus a thumb instead of 4 fingers, positioning the thumb forward from the wrist since palms face inward in a neutral A-pose.

Each finger gets a direction vector computed from spread angle and a downward curl, then two joint points are built along that direction, swept with tapering radius for a tapered cylindrical shape in skin tone, skipping fingernail detail.

I'm now working out the thumb base position and direction similarly, planning the per-hand joint chains with naming conventions tied to finger index and side, deciding which arm joint to attach the palm bone to, and adding a leather bracer cuff near the wrist as a separate cylinder.

For the gauntlet I'm considering small brass details -- rivets, a tiny dial, stud rows -- but settling on just one simple brass band to keep it clean. I'm also sketching out the eye position formula and starting to write a helper function to generate a gear-shaped outline for the back decoration.

Writing gear outline code...

Then I extrude that gear shape onto the body using the brass material, positioning it on the back near the bone joint.

Adding more pack details...

Checking the gear spacing against each other for clearance, then working through patch placements around the gears to avoid overlap, verifying bottom and side margins stay within bounds.

I'm placing rivets along the pack's perimeter inset from the edge, setting them at the rear face z-depth to align with the bevel, then writing the edge-rivet generation function that walks each polygon edge and spaces rivets evenly along it.

Now I'm building the telescope on the right side, stacking rod segments along the z-axis for the leather grip, brass barrel sections, and a glowing lens disc at the tip.

I'm checking that the telescope rod placement aligns properly against the pack outline so the strap rings connect them without gaps, verifying the geometry at different y positions.

Now I'm working out a brass spring coil attached to the lower pack side, positioning its center and radius so it touches the pack edge, then building it as a helical sweep with small tube segments and calculating how many rings are needed per turn to keep the curve smooth.

Adding end discs and a central steel guide rod for the spring, then shifting focus to the tank shape—adding a dome cap, reinforcing bands, rivet rows, and a sight glass detail.

Now I'm placing a glowing blue-green water-level gauge on the tank's outer side with a brass frame, plus a front-facing valve wheel, and giving the tank a mottled copper paint texture rather than a plain material. I'm also thinking about boiler chimney steam puffs and how the pipe connects to the rotor, then moving on to anchoring everything to the bone rig starting from the chest/spine joint.

For apron pocket details, I'm working out tool placement — small screwdriver-handle cylinders poking just above the pocket edge but tucked beneath the belt so only a sliver shows, adjusting heights so they don't clip into the belt geometry while still looking visible.

Alternatively, I'll hang tools from belt loops instead: a hammer and wrench plus two screwdrivers dangling at the front-left and front-right, each with a handle cylinder up top and a thin steel blade rod pointing down along the apron, colored red and yellow for variety. I'm skipping the chest pocket detail for simplicity.

Now I'm thinking about the lantern chain hinge and the fan rotor blades, working out the geometry for three blades spaced 120° apart with a tapered outline, using radial and tangent direction vectors and a cross product to determine the blade's thickness axis.

I'm figuring out how to paint the blade tips red while leaving the rest mustard colored, then placing the rotor hub and mast components -- a cylinder hub and a steel rod running from the lid top up to the rotor center, sized to fit the pack assembly proportions.

Adding the gnome nose as a small flat-shaded red icosphere, then checking part counts stay reasonable before writing the full build. I'm defining the joint hierarchy next -- neck, head, and jaw joints with their parent attachments, positions, and orientation vectors.

Still writing joint definitions...

I'm working out the hat and beard chains, parenting the hat to the head and the beard to the jaw, using a Catmull-Rom curve through station center points so the loft and chain share the same path, then naming the beard segments sequentially.

Now I'm defining the beard's shading with grain-based paint and setting the loft stations with width/height values that taper from the chin area down to a point, deciding on octagonal cross-sections with flat facets rather than smooth curves.

Checking that the beard's curved path doesn't awkwardly intersect the torso front or neck geometry at matching y-coordinates, verifying the radii line up reasonably against the chest's taper calculations.

I'm figuring out the apron straps now—deciding whether to bother modeling the straps crossing over the shoulders to the back, since most of that area will be hidden behind the beard anyway. Thinking it's cheaper to skip the detailed strap geometry there and just include a minimal stand-in piece.

Now I'm setting up the skirt as a lathe shape, giving it a flared cone-like profile that sits at the hips, using a dark teal color for contrast with the tunic, and checking that it's wide enough to fully cover the legs underneath down to where it ends.

I'm adding a small mustard-colored trim ring at the hem of the skirt for detail, then moving on to write the SVG texture for the dial face with concentric circles and brass coloring.

Still writing SVG code...

Still writing gear SVG...

Defining the spine chain and torso radius function...

Writing belt sweep code...

Adding brass buckle detail...

Now I'm moving to the head geometry, building the skull from an icosahedron shape attached to the head bone, then adding small blush-colored cheek spheres positioned symmetrically on either side of the face with flattened scaling for a subtle proud effect.

I'm now placing the eyes using small icosahedron whites with flattened pupils and tiny highlight dots, positioning them symmetrically along the x-axis relative to the head bone.

I'm sketching the eyebrows as curved catmull-rom sweeps above each eye with tapering radii, checking they sit under the hat brim without clipping.

Refining hat chain coordinates so the cone sits properly on the head, with total model height landing around 1.22m, then checking that goggles and decals at various heights stay clear of the head radius.

Calculating decal placement near y 1.12 against the hat's radius profile, then moving on to the mustache, nose, mouth, and ears. For the hat itself, I'm building a chain of points with Catmull-Rom interpolation and sweeping a tapering radius profile along it to form the hat's shape.

Still writing hat geometry... I'm now adding a small bell shape at the hat's tip, lathing a profile curve and positioning it hanging down near the pointed end of the hat chain.

For the band, I'm deciding to keep just a single strap element (the goggle strap at y=1.02) rather than layering a separate brass hat band, keeping the brim lathe as its own piece.

I'm defining a helper to build circular ring paths, then writing the lathe outline for the brim shape attached to the hat's first bone joint since it shouldn't bend, and sketching how the strap sweep geometry attaches using the catmull closed path helper.

Now I'm setting up the pack extrusion with a bevel and thickness attached to the chest bone, using an outline of points, and starting to think through whether side pockets are needed near the tank.

Moving to the top assembly: I'm placing the lid as a flat box with a hinge joint at the rear, adding a small brass lock at the front edge, and sketching strap boxes spanning across the lid at symmetric x positions.

The rotor mast should stay fixed to the chest bone rather than the lid, so it doesn't swing when the lid opens, and I'm checking the antenna base position to make sure it sits within the pack's top outline instead of floating beyond its edge.
